title: Who Designed the BEST UI/UX Cards?

best.what: white space inside buttons, consistent line-heights on headlines, cards feel thin/sparse if too spaced out
rule: a shadow must be darker than what it sits on, not lighter; simplify a busy watermarked card
decluttering: overlapping semi-transparent layers create noise, swap for simple flat icons

why: Rapid before/after fixes on real submissions -- white space, contrast, shadow logic, decluttering -- confirms the known pattern: review episodes are short, concrete design rules, not Figma clicking.

title: Designing Forms in Figma - UI/UX Challenge

best.what: minimum viable form: a contact form needs about 2-3 fields (name/email/message + submit), nothing more
why a text field needs a visible stroke/border for contrast against a light background -- an accessibility point, not decoration
a form field needs three states -- default, focus, error -- and what should visually change for each

why: Matches the known challenge-video pattern: a handful of good concepts up front (field count, contrast, default/focus/error), then 15+ minutes of Figma auto-layout/component-variant/prototype mechanics the kids will never do since Gemini builds the UI. Pull the three clips, skip the rest.

title: Who made the BEST UI/UX Layout from THIS Challenge?

best.what: a 'muddy' busy photo-watermark background fixed by stripping to flat color + high-contrast type, removing wide letter-spacing on sentences
closing summary of the whole episode in one breath: simplify, mind columns/rows, align with white space, don't throw things around randomly

why: Same review pattern as the cards episode confirmed again: real entries, fast simplify/align/contrast fixes, and a clean closing rule that's quotable on its own.

title: Who Designed the BEST Sub Page for this Layout?

best.what: decluttering a busy title treatment and tightening list-item spacing
a submission that added labels nobody asked for gets rejected outright -- scope creep as a UX mistake, not just a look problem
text wrapped to look clickable when it isn't -- a false-affordance mistake, the same idea Kole Jain's video names as 'signifiers'

why: Confirms the review pattern a third time; the scope-creep and false-affordance moments are genuinely transferable UX lessons, not just visual polish, and cross-link nicely to the Kole Jain video.

title: Designing Dashboards in Figma | UI/UX Challenge

best.what: what a dashboard needs: a sidebar nav, a date picker, and 3-4 headline stat numbers above a trend chart
stat cards laid out three-in-a-row above the chart to save vertical space -- a reusable dashboard layout idea

why: Fits the challenge pattern exactly: the requirements list is a good 'what goes on a stats page' checklist for a Sheets-backed dashboard, but the remaining ~14 minutes are Figma auto-layout, icon-plugin and chart-plugin clicking they will never do.

title: Every UI/UX Concept Explained in Under 10 Minutes

best.what: signifiers: grouping, a selected-state highlight, and greyed-out text all communicate function without any instructions
grids are optional, white space is not -- concrete spacing values for a simple hero section
every button needs 4 states (default/hover/active/disabled), inputs need focus/error states, and microinteractions confirm an action happened

why: The single best dense primer for this course: signifiers, hierarchy, white space, type, color, dark mode, icon sizing, UI states and microinteractions in under 10 minutes with concrete before/afters, and no tool-clicking to sit through.

title: How a web application works

best.what: plain split: HTML is the text, CSS is the appearance, JS is the interaction -- and that's the whole front-end/back-end line

MVC explained as three worker teams -- model handles the database, view is what the user sees, controller sits between them -- maps directly onto Sheet = model, HTML = view, Apps Script functions = controller

why: Adds one real thing the library's Academind and code.org videos don't cover: the MVC pattern, which maps cleanly onto their Sheets+Apps Script+HTML stack. But at 35 minutes it re-explains its own IKEA-store analogy at length and drifts into Docker/Kubernetes/AWS/enterprise-scaling territory the course doesn't need -- pull the two clips, skip the rest.

title: Create WBS Process and the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)

best.what: worked example: break a website project into deliverables (UX / servers / database, then pages/CSS/images, schema/tables) -- a hierarchical breakdown pattern they could copy for their own app

why: Fails the 14-year-old test for 16 of its 18 minutes: knowledge-area mapping, ITTO lists, a scope-baseline equation, and repeated PMP-exam and 'smash the like button' plugs -- none of it usable by a solo teen on a 4-8 week project. The one website-breakdown example is worth stealing for a 'how to break your project into pieces' guide page; nothing else earns a spot.
